notes.meaning: Job asks why God does not set public times for court and judgment, and why His faithful followers do not get to see those days. His friends argued that God instantly punishes every sinner, but Job points out that God's justice is often not seen right away in this world. God rules everything, but He tests our faith by choosing His own timing to settle accounts.

Evil men secretly move stone boundary markers to steal land from their neighbors. They also seize herds of animals by force and openly graze them as if they owned them. Because no judge stops them immediately, they carry on without fear of being caught.

Greedy people steal the donkey of an orphan child and take a poor widow's ox as a pledge, which is a deposit held until a debt is paid. Taking away these working beasts robs the most helpless people of their only way to plow and earn food. God cares deeply for orphans and widows, making this cruelty especially wicked.

Oppressors push needy people off the main roads and force the poor of the land into hiding. The vulnerable must scatter into caves and hills just to stay safe from violent men. Tolerating such abuse makes the whole society a worse place to live.

Job describes lawless outlaws who live like wild donkeys roaming the dry desert. They wake up early to hunt for prey and rob travelers along the highway. They treat raiding as their daily job to feed themselves and their children.

These raiders sweep across the countryside to harvest grain that belongs to others. They also strip the grapes from the vineyards of wicked landowners, showing that violent plunderers will even steal from other evil men. One crook ends up robbing another, yet both seem to get away with it.

The poor victims who were robbed are stripped of their outer garments and left to shiver through freezing desert nights. Drenched by heavy mountain downpours, they have no house and must cling to bare rocks for shelter. Their terrible suffering shows how cruel unchecked oppression really is.

Ruthless creditors tear a nursing baby away from its mother's breast to satisfy a debt. They take the child to raise as a slave because the poor family has nothing else left to pay. Greed drives these men to break every bond of natural love and mercy.

Cruel masters force poor laborers to carry heavy bundles of harvested grain while starving, and make them work without proper clothing. These workers squeeze olives into oil and stomp grapes in the winepresses, yet they are forbidden to take even a sip to quench their thirst. The rich enjoy luxury while withholding the basic fruits of labor from those who do the work.

Cries of agony rise from the city, where wounded and dying people groan under heavy extortion. Even so, God does not step in at once or brand the abusers as fools before the world. Job is troubled by this silence, yet he knows God never overlooks evil forever.

Job turns to a group of sinners who rebel against the light. They refuse to walk in the light of God's truth, their own conscience, or the clear day itself. They deliberately choose darkness because they know their actions are wrong.

The murderer rises at the break of dawn to ambush helpless travelers on their way to work or market. He is willing to take a human life just to steal a small amount of money or goods. When night arrives, he slips through the streets like a thief to keep on stealing.

The adulterer waits eagerly for evening twilight, telling himself that no one will spot him. He wraps a veil or mask over his face so he will not be recognized on his way to break marriage vows. Sinners go to great lengths to hide from other people while foolishly forgetting that God sees all.

Thieves dig through the soft mud walls of houses in the pitch dark, but they lock themselves inside as soon as morning comes. Bright daylight feels as dreadful to them as the shadow of death because they might be caught and punished. They make friends with nighttime terrors and run away from the light of day.

Job observes how quickly the wicked man passes away, like light foam swept down a river. After his death, the estate he left behind is recognized as cursed by God, and no one visits his pleasant vineyards. His earthly glory disappears without trace.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest Job is quoting his friends' viewpoint here to set up an argument against it, rather than stating his own belief.

notes.meaning: Just as dry soil and summer heat quickly dry up melted snow, the grave swallows up those who have sinned. They slip out of life easily and quietly, without facing the sudden public doom that Job's friends claimed always happens. Death is the common end that overtakes them all.

Even his own mother soon forgets him, and worms feed on his body in the grave like any ordinary corpse. He is not remembered with honor, and his wicked power is snapped like a fallen tree. His proud life ends in complete ruin and silence.

In life, this man abused childless women who had no sons to defend them against bullies. He also refused to give any help to the struggling widow, adding pain to people who were already hurting. His lack of pity toward the helpless explains why nobody mourns him when he dies.

A cruel tyrant uses his immense power to drag even strong men into his net. When he rises up in sudden anger, nobody around him can feel sure of staying alive. Yet despite terrifying everyone, he often keeps his grip on power for years.

God allows these evil men to feel safe and comfortable for a time, but His eyes never leave their ways. The wicked mistake God's patience for approval, not realizing that He is keeping record of everything they do. God sees every hidden deed and will judge it at the right time.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: The Latin Vulgate reads this verse as God granting the sinner time to repent, which the wicked man foolishly abuses through his own pride.

notes.meaning: Wicked men are lifted up in honor for a short life, and then they die like everyone else. Instead of being dragged out by public disasters, they often pass away quietly in old age, like ripe heads of wheat snipped off at harvest. Their success in this life proves that earthly comfort is no proof of a person's goodness.

Job finishes his speech by challenging anyone present to prove him wrong or show that his argument is empty. Daily life clearly proves that bad people often prosper while good people suffer. Job knows his words match real experience, whereas his friends' simple rules do not hold up.
